articles.title: Supreme Court pushes back against Trump and GOP ahead of the midterm elections
articles.summary: The Supreme Court delivered major blows to President Donald Trump and Republicans, suggesting it will not be receptive to last-minute election changes heading into the midterms.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court in the last week has delivered major blows to President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans that suggest the justices will not be receptive to last-minute efforts to change election rules heading into the midterms. With control of Congress at stake, the court on Monday night blocked Trump’s plan to exert federal control over mail-in ballots via a Postal Service regulation. The decision came after the court twice last week ruled against Republicans by declining to revive a new congressional map in Missouri that would have eliminated one of two Democratic-held districts. While the court has a 6-3 conservative majority that often rules for Republican priorities, there are limits to how receptive some justices are to more extreme requests, election law experts told NBC News. That’s especially true for cases that could disrupt voters when an election is close or already underway. Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor and election law expert at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, said the recent decisions show “there aren’t five votes for abject chaos.” “I think the court is going to pay very close attention to any extraordinary actions that destabilize the electoral process,” said Bob Bauer, who served as White House counsel under President Barack Obama. “There’s a signal here that this sort of late intervention is going to receive scrutiny.” On the left, the Supreme Court has been viewed with particular distrust and alarm as it relates to election issues following a major ruling in the spring that further weakened the landmark Voting Rights Act. In the aftermath, the court quickly allowed Republican states to draw new congressional maps that eliminated majority-Black, Democratic-held seats. But now it is Trump who appears angered and frustrated by the court’s actions. “It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself, and makes cheating by the Radical Left ‘Dumocrats,’ on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do — And now they have an open field to do so!” he said in a Truth Social post on Tuesday, repeating his unfounded claims about widespread election fraud. With some states already sending out ballots for the midterm elections, timing was an issue for Republicans in both cases. The Missouri Supreme Court faulted Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins for delaying a decision on whether the new map could be challenged, ultimately finding him in contempt for defying its ruling in favor of plaintiffs. As for the Postal Service, it pushed through the new regulation despite concerns raised by election officials that they would be unable to implement it in time. “In both instances, the court said we’re not going to countenance that,” said Travis Crum, an NBC News contributor and law professor at Washington University in St. Louis. “I do think that the Missouri case is going to send the message that dragging your feet like this is not going to be rewarded by the Supreme Court.” As the November elections loom, efforts to make late changes to the rules, including any new proposals from the Trump administration relating to mail-in ballots, are likely to meet with a similarly frosty reception from the justices, experts said. They cautioned, though, that it is too early to say what new litigation could arise ahead of or after Election Day. Among the concerns that have been raised by some election officials are that the Trump administration could post federal immigration agents near polling places, although officials have said they have no current plans to do so. As he has done previously, Trump might also complain about mail-in ballots being counted after in-person votes, claiming voter fraud because the outcome might appear to change, even though it is customary for various jurisdictions to continue counting ballots after Election Day under state law. States with competitive elections, especially those that could determine control of the Senate, could be a particular focus for any Election Day or post-election litigation. These include Texas and Georgia, two states under Republican control with competitive races. Alaska, where votes often take a long time to count, is another state that could attract litigation, with Democrats hoping to win the Senate race there. One fear among election administrators is that the federal government could try to seize ballots and other voting records over claims of election fraud similar to those Trump and his allies raised, and courts rejected, following the 2020 presidential election. In January, the FBI searched an election office in Georgia, seizing 2020 election ballots. But as the Supreme Court has shown in other cases, the conservative majority follows its own agenda, not Trump’s, and has delivered him major defeats this year on his sweeping tariffs and plan to roll back birthright citizenship. “This court is radically conservative,” Levitt said, “but not actually in the tank for Trump’s particular version of personalist chaos.”

articles.title: Dem leaders warn against AI companies policing themselves: ‘We need Congress to act’
articles.summary: Top House Democrats warned Tuesday that AI companies can’t be trusted to regulate themselves, arguing that the federal government will have to step in with industry-wide rules designed to ensure public safety. “This is not an industry that can regulate itself,” Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, told reporters in the…
articles.body:
Top House Democrats warned Tuesday that AI companies can’t be trusted to regulate themselves, arguing that the federal government will have to step in with industry-wide rules designed to ensure public safety.

“This is not an industry that can regulate itself,” Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, told reporters in the Capitol. “We have the ability, and we should be regulating them and putting sensible guardrails to protect consumers while supporting an innovation economy.”

The remarks clash with the message coming from top Republicans, who say members of Congress are simply not equipped to regulate the AI industry on their own, given the sheer complexity of the technology that makes AI tick.

“Congress is obviously less qualified than the people who are pushing this frontier to know all the ins and outs of it,” House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union” program.

Johnson wants to sit down with AI leaders as early as this week to gauge their view of potential restrictions and Congress’s role in installing them.

Democrats say the Speaker’s position is a classic case of the fox guarding the henhouse. They want the House, which is scheduled to leave Washington this week for a long midterm break, to remain in town to hash out legislation that prioritizes public safety.

“We have an obligation to protect the American public, and that’s what we should be doing by creating guardrails and rules of the road,” Aguilar said. “This is our job. If we’re not up to speed, then it’s on each member to get up to speed. And it’s unfortunate that the Speaker thinks so low of this institution.”

The concerns surrounding AI have exploded in recent days in the wake of a public statement from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who warned that AI technology is moving faster than the industry’s capacity to control it. He said Anthropic will voluntarily slow down that development, and urged other companies to do the same or risk a global catastrophe.

Two other titans of the AI world, Sam Altman and Elon Musk, endorsed Amodei’s message.

The warning has caused an uproar on Capitol Hill, where Democrats, and some Republicans, are calling for immediate action to adopt new AI safeguards.

President Trump, however, has rejected the idea of adopting tougher rules for the industry, arguing that such limits would disadvantage American companies in the race for global AI dominance.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” Trump wrote Monday on X . “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”

Democrats acknowledge that any regulations adopted by Congress would not extend beyond America’s borders. With that in mind, Rep. Ted Lieu (Calif.), the vice chairman of the House Democratic Congress, urged Trump to press Chinese leaders to commit to a ban on AI systems launching nuclear weapons, which became law in the U.S. in the last Congress.

“There are things that we can do to get other countries to follow the lead the U.S. has taken in AI,” Lieu said.

In the meantime, Lieu called on all AI companies to follow Anthropic’s example and tap the brakes on development.

“Until they can make their AI models and agents safe, so they don’t go rogue or go hack other companies, they need to slow down their development and put in adequate guardrails,” Lieu said.

“And we cannot expect the industry to regulate itself. We need Congress to act.”

articles.title: Prosecutors drop death penalty for Nick Reiner for alleged murders of parents
articles.summary: The couple was found stabbed to death in their Southern California home in late 2025.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Prosecutors are no longer seeking the death penalty against Nick Reiner, who is accused in the double murders of his parents, director Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner .

Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman announced his decision Tuesday, saying the maximum sentence Reiner can now receive is life in prison without the possibility of parole if convicted.

Hochman said he had discussed taking the death penalty off the table with Reiner’s siblings before making the decision.

The son had previously been charged with first-degree murder , but prosecutors secured a special circumstance enhancement that alleges he was lying in wait to murder them. The special circumstance can increase potential penalties in the sentencing phase of a trial to life in prison without parole.

He was indicted by a grand jury last month. The indictment will expedite the case to a jury, bypassing a preliminary hearing.

Reiner had previously pleaded not guilty to the killings of his parents.

Rob and Michele Singer Reiner honored at the Emmys

Rob Reiner was honored during the Emmy Awards on Monday night.

Actress Jamie Lee Curtis gave a tribute to Rob Reiner, who won a posthumous award for outstanding guest actor in a comedy series for his appearance in FX’s “The Bear.”

“He was generous and kind and funny as hell and a friend to all,” Curtis said.

The couple was found stabbed to death in their Southern California home after their daughter discovered them in late 2025. Reiner was later arrested and jailed without bail in connection with the murders.

Documents from the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health stated the couple died within “minutes” of receiving “multiple sharp force injuries” with a “knife, by another.”

Reiner, who lived with his parents, had previously spoken openly about his struggles with drug addiction and periods of homelessness and co-wrote a movie inspired by his struggles with his father.

articles.title: Judge rejects bid to put Trump's name on Kennedy Center building
articles.summary: The ruling came as the centre's Trump-appointed board was reportedly scheduled to vote on closing it for two years.
articles.body:
The Kennedy Center board has voted to close the performing arts centre for two years, just as a US judge blocked it from adding President Donald Trump's name back to the building.

In May, the same judge ordered the removal of Trump's name and blocked its temporary closure for proposed renovations

The board, which is chaired by Trump and comprises his cabinet members and allies, approved a resolution in August that called for the inscription "Renovated and Restored by President Donald J. Trump" to be added to the venue.

Trump announced the addition of his name to the institution, among other rebranding measures across the nation's capital, last year.

The judge's written order came less than an hour before the centre's board voted on the closure.

This was the third time it has approved closing the centre since February, amid legal challenges to Trump's work to take greater control of the institution, and there is a chance the centre's doors could stay open despite Tuesday's vote.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that the board voted "almost unanimously" to close the storied venue "for safety reasons" and to begin the process of reconstruction.

While the closing "will take place immediately", Trump said renovations cannot begin until the court "rules on the Board's approved name" and vowed to take the case to the Supreme Court if it is a "negative" ruling.

He added that the US Department of Justice will ask for an expedited appeal and that he had raised $17m for the centre to "keep it afloat".

Also in August, the board approved a resolution to rename the campus the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza" if $100m was raised for the renovations.

Congress approved more than $250m for renovations in Trump's massive spending legislation known as "The Big Beautiful Bill".

However, the centre cannot close unless the federal judge, Christopher Cooper, lifts a temporary block that he put in place in May requiring it to stay open while a lawsuit brought by board member Joyce Beatty goes ahead.

When he put the block in place, Cooper said the board could return and request it be lifted, provided it had come to the decision to close "in a prudent manner". The justice department is expected to make that request by Friday, CNN reported.

Beatty, an Ohio congresswoman and Democrat, said on Tuesday that the centre had planned to undergo phased renovations for years while still putting on some performances, instead of fully shuttering.

She blamed Trump's attempt to rename the centre for the departure of donors, patrons, and artists.

"Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity," she said in a statement to the BBC. "That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee. Congress established the Kennedy Center as a living memorial to President Kennedy, and I am proud to defend this cherished institution."

In February 2025, Trump replaced several trustees on the board, which then decided in December to rename the institution. New lettering bearing Trump's full name was affixed to the centre's front portico the following day.

The changes, including the re-naming, were followed by cancellations by artists booked at the venue and a drop in ticket sales.

Most of the legal challenges to Trump's changes focus on the fact that Congress established the centre as a memorial to President John F Kennedy, who was assassinated in 1963. While detractors say that means Congress must approve changes to the memorial, Trump has argued that he has the power to act.

"Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing," Judge Cooper said in a written order issued on Tuesday.

The judge said the board's proposal to add language to the existing name of the centre and its surrounding campus "bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted".

That statute was a decision by the US legislative body to memorialise Kennedy, "and no one else, at the Center bearing his name", the order said.

On Sunday, the Kennedy Center administration told its board that the arts institution was on the brink of bankruptcy, the Washington Post reported.

The administration said it was in a "precarious fiscal position" and would not be able to support its payroll obligations and routine maintenance contracts "within a matter of weeks".

The current leadership at the centre has said the building is unsafe for continued occupancy, pointing to part of the ceiling falling in earlier this month. But others close to the centre dispute that it must be closed.

The Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump said on Truth Social that the Kennedy Center is "in a virtual state of collapse".

He described dire conditions and railed against the "hostile and conflicted" judge for keeping it open despite not having performances scheduled or "people that would have the Courage to even go in".

articles.title: GOP Rep Thomas Massie introduces 8 articles of impeachment against War Secretary Pete Hegseth
articles.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie read eight articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth on the House floor, citing War Powers Resolution violations in Iran.
articles.body: Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced a resolution to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and read eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on the House floor Tuesday. Massie formally entered a resolution to impeach Hegseth for "high crimes and misdemeanors" on the House floor for, among other things, allegedly violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973 in Iran and for his role in the operation that led to former Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro's capture and extradition. The first three of the eight articles of impeachment Massie introduced accused Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973, arguing that Hegseth's Department of War is "waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat." His first article seeks to establish "that the war was unlawful from its inception." The second article claims that Hegseth disobeyed Congress after both the House and the Senate directed the removal of troops from Iran. The third article claims that Hegseth is "continuing hostilities in Iran after expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period." 4 HOUSE REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO BLOCK IRAN WAR POWERS The fourth and fifth articles accuse Hegseth of refusing to minimize civilian casualties and engaging in extrajudicial killing, with the latter charge accusing Hegseth of "replacing maritime law enforcement with unauthorized lethal military targeting of suspected drug traffickers" during operations striking suspected narcotraffickers in the Caribbean Sea. REP SETH MOULTON SAYS HEGSETH IS 'GUILTY' OF WAR CRIMES, LINKS HIM TO NAZIS TRIED DURING WORLD WAR II Also related to military action in the Caribbean and South America, Massie's seventh article accuses Hegseth of the "Kidnapping of a Sovereign Foreign Leader" for his role in Operation Absolute Resolve, the January mission in which U.S. Special Forces apprehended and extracted former Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores from Caracas. Massie's article condemns Hegseth for doing so "without constitutional or legal authority." Article six accuses Hegseth of using his authority to suppress the free speech of Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., by retaliating against the senator for his video in which the senator joined a group of other lawmakers in a video which critics claimed encourage active military members to disobey lawful orders. The final article charges Hegseth with carrying out unlawful orders in Yemen. The article "charges Secretary Hegseth with initiating Operation Rough Rider without congressional authorization or an imminent threat to the United States, while also violating war powers reporting requirements. It further addresses extensive civilian deaths and unlawful strikes on civilian objects, rescuers, and other protected persons." After reading out his articles for over an hour on the House floor, Massie closed out his introduction. "In all of this, Secretary Hegseth abused the powers entrusted to him as Secretary of Defense by subordinating the constitutional limits on the use of military force and the laws governing the conduct of hostilities to his own policy objectives," Massie said. Massie also added that Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to civilians, the lawful conduct of United States military operations, the integrity and credibility of the United States Armed Forces and the Constitution, if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties, and the rule of law. This, Massie said, "warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States." articles.title: Republicans may gain nothing from redistricting: DDHQ
articles.summary: Republicans aiming to gain seats in Congress after several GOP-controlled states redrew their congressional maps in the last year may gain nothing in the November midterm elections, according to the election handicapper Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). DDHQ’s election forecast on Tuesday shows Democrats having a 68 percent probability of winning the House compared to Republicans’…
articles.body:
Republicans aiming to gain seats in Congress after several GOP-controlled states redrew their congressional maps in the last year may gain nothing in the November midterm elections, according to the election handicapper Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

DDHQ’s election forecast on Tuesday shows Democrats having a 68 percent probability of winning the House compared to Republicans’ 32 percent.

“In Decision Desk HQ’s forecast, Democrats not only achieve an average gain of 13 seats in the states with unchanged boundaries, they also gain an average of two seats across the nine states that redistricted,” DDHQ chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley wrote on Substack .

Democrats won an average seat majority of 229-206 across the forecast’s 1 million simulations, resulting in a 14-seat gain, Skelley wrote. But factoring in the states with redrawn congressional maps, he said that Democrats make an average gain of 13 seats in the 41 states that did not redistrict, which Skelley emphasized as being the party’s “path to a majority.”

“In our forecast for the unchanged states, Democrats win an average of nearly 150 seats, up from the 137 they currently control,” he continued. “Meanwhile, the redistricted states do not come close to offsetting that shift.”

He explained how in Texas, “Republicans are averaging a bit under a two-seat gain, roughly three seats short of their ideal.” Texas was the first state to redraw its map after President Trump urged red states to redistrict in order to maintain and increase their majority in Congress, with other red states following suit.

Redrawn districts that are home to Latino majorities give Texas Democratic incumbents a slight advantage, with Reps. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) and Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) both forecasted to keep their seats.

“Similarly, they also have around a 1 in 3 chance of defeating two-term GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in the 15th District,” Skelley continued. “While Trump would have won that seat by roughly 18 points under the new lines, he only would have won it by about two points in 2020.”

Florida could also see Republicans underperform more, with no shift favoring Republicans despite redistricting targeting four Democratic-held seats, with at least two of those seats both being favorites to hold on, Skelley wrote.

Ohio holds a similar likelihood of underperforming, with three Democrats likely to keep their seats and Rep. Max Miller’s (R-Ohio) district shifting toward a toss-up amid allegations of domestic abuse in connection with his wife.

The first Democratic-led state to retaliate with its own ballot measure to redraw its map could give California four seats out of the five where it could see gains. But Skelley said that Rep. David Valadao (R-Calif.) is the “smaller underdog” on “turf that Trump narrowly would have won in 2024” in the 22nd District.

“A potential Republican win there, as well as outside shots in districts such as the 13th, 45th, and GOP-held 48th [districts] help keep Democrats from averaging the full-on five-seat gain they want in California,” Skelley added.

Missouri has been the latest front in the redistricting battle. The state’s Supreme Court earlier this month unanimously ruled that the redrawn map designed to benefit Republicans “did not go into effect and will not go into effect” unless voters approve it in a referendum in the fall.

Skelley said DDHQ has a freeze on Missouri’s forecast until the legal battle over the map “is finalized.”

The high court said that the state must use the old map that favored the GOP six seats to two rather than replace it with the 7-1 House map used during this year’s primaries. The decision has confused Missouri voters as to which primary candidates will appear on the ballot. It has also made them angry, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-Mo.) previously told The Hill.

Trump called the ruling a “Dark Day for ‘Justice’ in Missouri” and claimed that the election process had been, “as usual … disturbed.”

articles.title: Iran war driving up inflation for Americans, CBO report says
articles.summary: The Congressional Budget Office estimates the war with Iran is the cause of more than one-third of the increase in inflation this year and that it will cause further increases in the first quarter of next year, according to a new report released Tuesday.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The war with Iran is driving up inflation and borrowing costs may increase for Americans, according to a new report released Tuesday by the Congressional Budget Office. The report found the war was responsible for more than one-third of the increase in inflation this year, and inflation will likely continue to grow in the first quarter of next year. The CBO specifically blames the war for more than 40% of inflation during the second quarter of 2026 and an estimated half a percentage point of higher inflation during the first quarter of 2027. Interest rates are likely to rise as a result, making borrowing more costly the report found. Interest rates are likely to keep rising as a result, making borrowing more costly, the report found. The rate on the typical 30-year mortgage was under 6% before the war started; it’s at 7.22% as of Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Wall Street, likewise, expects the Federal Reserve to raise its key interest rate Wednesday in a bid to tamp down inflation. The main driver of increased inflation is fewer oil and natural gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, the CBO report says. The average price of a gallon of gasoline in the U.S. is up 45% since the beginning of the war, hitting $4.32 as of Tuesday. Diesel, which is essential to the economy as it fuels farm equipment and other commercial vehicles, has increased 66% to a record $6.26. The Congressional Budget Office is a nonpartisan federal agency controlled by Congress that conducts analysis related to the federal budget and the economy. The estimate comes a day after the Pentagon’s watchdog found the Iran war resulted in a shortfall of U.S. munitions and “bottlenecks” in supply chains. The CBO report estimates it will be five years before the Pentagon is able to replace munitions expended during the war, which it estimates has cost roughly $38 billion as of Aug. 1. That cost estimate does not include the price tag for repairing damage Iran inflicted on “hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases” in the Middle East. The Pentagon didn’t cooperate with requests from CBO, according to the agency. “For 47 years, American Presidents and countless other world leaders talked about the threat posed by Iran, but no one had the courage to address it,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement. “President Trump took decisive action to ensure that Iran could never harm our homeland, our troops, or our allies again. The United States Military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief’s strategic goals and beyond.” One of the reasons the CBO says it could not estimate the cost of damage to U.S. military bases and other facilities in the region is because the Defense Department hasn’t shared with the office “information about the value of damaged or destroyed equipment and property” or what repairs the Pentagon plans to make, the funding for which could in part be picked up by the countries where the facilities are located. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., in a written statement called for an end to the war and described it as “a one-two punch that’s burning a hole in Americans’ pockets and burning a hole in our munitions supply, hurting our military readiness.” The report estimated it would cost $13.1 billion to replace missile defense interceptors alone, and the overall cost to replace munitions expended through Aug. 1 would be $21.7 billion. It will take roughly $2 billion to $3 billion per month to maintain the war’s status quo, and more if the conflict escalates, the report found.

articles.title: Talarico leads Paxton by 3 points in new Texas Senate poll
articles.summary: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico (D) is still leading his GOP challenger, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, according to a new poll released Tuesday. The Telemundo/Mason-Dixon Polling & Research survey found the Democrat, a Texas state representative, held a three-point advantage over his Republican opponent less than two months out before November’s midterms. Forty-six…
articles.body:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico (D) is still leading his GOP challenger, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, according to a new poll released Tuesday.

The Telemundo /Mason-Dixon Polling & Research survey found the Democrat, a Texas state representative, held a three-point advantage over his Republican opponent less than two months out before November’s midterms.

Forty-six percent of the Texas voters surveyed supported the state lawmaker, while 43 percent backed the attorney general.

Additionally, three percent of respondents indicated they would vote for Libertarian Party candidate Ted Brown, and the remaining 8 percent said they were still undecided.

Talarico notably posted a strong lead among independent respondents, 51 percent of whom said they would support him over Paxton — who garnered just 30 percent of their backing. Thirteen percent of independents said they had yet to make up their mind about who they would vote for in this race.

The state representative also had an 18-point advantage among Hispanic voters and 75-point edge with Black voters against his Republican opponent. Among white respondents, Paxton had an 18-point lead.

The Democrat has generally pulled ahead of Paxton after the Texas attorney general beat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the state’s GOP primary runoff in May. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, shifted its rating for this race from “leans Republican” to a “toss up” after Cornyn’s defeat.

Two June Siena University polls found the two candidates tied, first at 46 and then at 47 percent. By the end of July, Talarico had pulled ahead of Paxton by four percentage points in this polling center’s survey.

Paxton had a narrow one-point advantage over the Democrat in an Emerson College poll conducted in early August, earning 47 percent of respondents’ support.

Almost a quarter of Texas voters Telemundo surveyed, 24 percent, said economic factors would most motivate how they cast their vote in the midterm races. Other major issues respondents identified were inflation and living costs — amounting for 23 percent of responses — as well as immigration at 18 percent.

Economic concerns have been top of mind for voters across the nation this election cycle, amid surging energy prices during the ongoing Iran war and President Trump’s tariff fight with Canada.

The Telemundo poll was conducted among a total of 625 registered Texas voters from Sept. 8-10 with an approximately 4 percentage point error margin.

articles.title: Kennedy Center board votes to close main building for renovations
articles.summary: The Kennedy Center board voted Tuesday to immediately close the venue’s main building for renovations, according to a source familiar, as the board argues that only President Trump can raise enough money to save it. The vote comes after officials indicated that the performing arts center faces “certain fiscal collapse within weeks,” with a draft…
articles.body:
The Kennedy Center board voted Tuesday to immediately close the venue’s main building for renovations, according to a source familiar, as the board argues that only President Trump can raise enough money to save it.

The vote comes after officials indicated that the performing arts center faces “certain fiscal collapse within weeks,” with a draft resolution describing the center as on the brink of bankruptcy, soon to be unable to make payroll or routine maintenance contracts.

The board, handpicked by Trump, has also said the building was “unsafe for continued occupancy,” pointing to a recent water leak that caused a partial collapse of the grand foyer ceiling.

Trump said after the vote that the closure “will take place immediately” but that the work can’t be done until the D.C. Circuit rules on the center’s name change to include his name.

“If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” he wrote on Truth Social. “The attorneys from the DOJ will ask for an expedited appeal.”

“In the meantime, 17 Million Dollars, raised by President Trump, has been put into The Kennedy Center account to keep it afloat,’ he added.

Trump reportedly attended the vote virtually.

Minutes before the vote was scheduled to take place, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper again blocked the board’s attempt to add Trump’s name to the facade. It was the second time that the judge found the board’s action was likely unlawful.

“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” Cooper wrote. “The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.”

The resolutions point to Trump’s fundraising skills as the center’s only saving grace. The board of trustees was restructured by the president last February, when he fired half the board and installed 14 new members.

“The Board understands that without such appropriate recognition it is unlikely that President Trump will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building and lead the fiscal rescue of the Center,” the resolution stated.

Justice Department attorneys, who are representing the Kennedy Center in the ongoing legal challenge, told Cooper during a hearing last month that the center was in “structural and financial disarray,” arguing further court intervention would impede the renovation project.

Cooper rejected that notion as “not quite fair,” noting that his initial order in late May allowed “necessary maintenance and repair work” to continue.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said last month that the renovations are expected to cost $257 million. He also said the proposed renovations would keep open the REACH, a new art space on the center’s campus, walking back previous controversial proposals that included its full closure.

Trump’s name was added to the Kennedy Center earlier this year after a board vote in December 2025. But there was outrage over the addition of the Trump name, and Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member, brought a lawsuit to stop the name change.

The president’s name was stripped from the building in June after a ruling said it violated federal law, but in August, the board voted on a resolution that would re-add Trump’s name in the form of two inscriptions.

Beatty on Tuesday said the decision to close the center is a “breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee.”

“For years, the Kennedy Center has planned to undergo phased renovations, in which we both renovate and maintain some performances. This is how major performing arts centers in the country operate. But donors, patrons, and artists all fled after the unlawful attempt to rename this sacred memorial after Donald Trump,” she said. “Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity. That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee.”

articles.title: ‘I’m not going to be a Republican!’: John Fetterman promises, again, not to defect
articles.summary: Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., insisted he won’t become a Republican, showing frustration with the ongoing questions about his intentions.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., insisted Tuesday he won’t become a Republican, showing frustration with the ongoing questions about his intentions. “I’m not going to be a Republican!” Fetterman said to reporters on Capitol Hill, raising his voice and shaking his head. “If I turn a Republican, then I’ll be a liar.” “My name is not on the ballot. Like, chill and wait for the midterm here,” he added. “I’ve always been a Democrat. It’s like, no matter how many times I say that, I’m still getting asked just getting into the elevator.” Fetterman, first elected in 2022, has grown increasingly distant from his party, mainly over his impassioned and unyielding defense of Israel and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He’s a regular guest on Fox News, where he gets asked about left-wing members of the Democratic Party and readily whacks them. Those positions and actions have drawn significant attention on Fetterman as a Democrat, but would become far less remarkable if he defected to the GOP. Fetterman sparked the speculation in mid-July when he opened the door to leaving the Democratic Party if it “officially” became “anti-Israel” in the party platform. As Republicans invited him to defect, he wondered aloud to NBC News days later whether Democrats still want him in the party. In response, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called Fetterman “a very good member of Congress” and one Democrats respect. The speculation arose again last week when Fetterman made a video appearance at the two-day Republican midterm convention in Dallas to introduce his “friend,” Sen. David McCormick, R-Pa. Fetterman issued a statement shortly after that saying he won’t switch parties if Democrats capture Senate control in November. His seat comes up for re-election in 2028, and Fetterman’s prospects of winning renomination as a Democrat are rapidly fading. A New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll last month found Fetterman’s approval rating among Democrats was just 22%, having fallen precipitously from 74% in May 2024. Yet, despite his rising approval rating among Pennsylvania Republicans in the same poll, his prospects of winning a GOP primary may be even more remote. Fetterman would have to defend his wide array of liberal positions — on matters such as expanding health care access, raising the federal minimum wage, supporting LGBTQ rights and championing legal abortion. On Tuesday, Fetterman ignored questions about a recently created X account reportedly run by his former staffers who have turned against him. He also declined to comment on a recent Wall Street Journal report detailing examples of Fetterman showing a lack of interest in doing the job of a senator, citing interviews with more than a dozen former staffers and lawmakers. Neither he nor his office commented for that story, but Fetterman called its reporting “smears” in a statement to CNN. One person who was quick to defend Fetterman was McCormick. “These stories are the latest example of outrageously disloyal staff and forces on the Left using anonymous leaks to cancel my friend John Fetterman,” he said on X. “They hate that he is an independent thinker who refuses to fall into line so they want to silence him.”

articles.title: Blanche dismisses concerns about Trump Jr’s wedding gift from Putin ally
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche dismissed concerns over a wedding gift to Donald Trump Jr. from an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier this year. “The president’s son has said that he’s a very close friend, and that he accepted a gift in the weekend of his wedding,” Blanche told reporters at the White House…
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche dismissed concerns over a wedding gift to Donald Trump Jr. from an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier this year.

“The president’s son has said that he’s a very close friend, and that he accepted a gift in the weekend of his wedding,” Blanche told reporters at the White House press briefing when asked if it was appropriate for Trump Jr. to accept the gift and if he would investigate if everything was appropriately reported as a gift.

“When you say ‘am I investigating?’ Am I investigating what? And when you say this person is a friend of Putin, I don’t even know if that’s true or not,” he continued. “I like that it’s fun to talk about this issue and the rhetoric around it, but I think all of the relevant people involved, the president and his kids have already addressed it.”

“I don’t have any information. I don’t know this person either,” he said.

ProPublica reported on Monday that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev funded Trump Jr. and wife Bettina Anderson’s lavish wedding festivities in the Bahamas, which included a private island and a fireworks show.

Democrats and critics were quick to lash out at the Trump administration over potential ethics violations and national security concerns.

Anderson, who is now Bettina Trump, responded to the fallout over the report in an Instagram post defending the wedding.

“Our friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding,” the post read. “It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.”

The president did not attend the wedding, but said in a statement to the New York Times that he had “no idea” who Kremlev was and said that the Russian oligarch “didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day.”

articles.title: Trump disses ‘hostile and conflicted’ judge who blocked Kennedy Center renaming
articles.summary: President Trump on Tuesday slammed the federal judge who blocked his administration’s latest effort to add his name to the Kennedy Center. The president, who has repeatedly criticized judges who rule against his administration, called U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper a “very hostile and conflicted Judge” shortly after the Obama appointee released his opinion in…
articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday slammed the federal judge who blocked his administration’s latest effort to add his name to the Kennedy Center.

The president, who has repeatedly criticized judges who rule against his administration, called U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper a “very hostile and conflicted Judge” shortly after the Obama appointee released his opinion in this case.

“Isn’t that too bad? We have already wasted more than 6 months ‘playing around’ in Court,” the president wrote on Truth Social . “Time is our Enemy! The Board, comprised of some of the most prominent and respected people in our Nation, is meeting again today. It will be interesting to see what happens.”

The president said the iconic performing arts center is “in a virtual state of collapse,” citing the recent damage to the Kennedy Center’s Grand Foyer ceiling after a heavy rain storm in the nation’s capital.

Cooper ruled Tuesday that the performing arts center’s board could not move forward with these renaming plans until it gets “Congress’s blessing” and found that the board’s August vote approving the addition of Trump’s name likely violated his earlier injunction.

The federal judge ruled in May that the president’s name must be removed from the building’s facade. Trump’s Justice Department made several unsuccessful attempts to pause this order, and the lettering was ultimately removed in June.

The Trump administration has exerted pressure to make a series of changes to the Kennedy Center. Last year, the president removed half of the center’s traditionally-bipartisan board, replaced these members with allies to his administration and named himself as the new chair.

These changes have been opposed by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member who challenged the Trump administration in a lawsuit.

“The law is extremely clear: The John F. Kennedy Center is named for President Kennedy — and no one else. But President Trump is holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial,” Beatty said in a statement following Cooper’s ruling.

“The Court just rejected this proposal for the second time,” she continued. “This unlawfulness is as breathtaking as it is wrong, and it needs to stop.”

articles.title: Blanche dodges question on whether he asked for DiGenova’s resignation
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche dodged a question Tuesday about whether he asked for the resignation of Trump-ally Joe diGenova from the Justice Department amid reports that there was a tense phone call between the two before the lawyer’s departure. “I don’t want to talk about communications I have with prosecutors. It’s not fair to them.…
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche dodged a question Tuesday about whether he asked for the resignation of Trump-ally Joe diGenova from the Justice Department amid reports that there was a tense phone call between the two before the lawyer’s departure.

“I don’t want to talk about communications I have with prosecutors. It’s not fair to them. It’s not fair to the process,” Blanche told reporters as he led a White House press briefing in the Rose Garden.

“He resigned last week. He came out of retirement to help the president, and to help us and we are very appreciative of the work that he did,” he continued.

DiGenova was tapped in April to lead an investigation into several of President Trump’s perceived enemies. He resigned last week, suggesting he was being asked to move too fast on the cases.

Asked why he resigned, diGenova told The Associated Press: “There’s plenty of evidence in all of these cases to prove the theories of prosecution. It just takes time to get there, and some people want to get there a little faster than others — and you can’t do that.”

In another interview with the New York Post, he said: “If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem.”

CNN reported Monday that diGenova resigned a day after a tense phone conversation with Blanche, citing sources familiar.

Blanche noted that diGenova said “some different things to different outlets, which is fine.”

“I very much appreciate the work that he did for us and for the administration,” he said. “Any investigations that he’s working of course continue, like they do, like any investigation does when somebody leaves. And we’re not going to slow down just because somebody leaves.”

Prosecutors on the case have reportedly focused on former CIA Director John Brennan and have also pursued information about those who worked on the Mar-a-Lago classified documents case against the president during the Biden administration.

articles.title: House Democrats demand answers from CDC on Pennsylvania measles deaths
articles.summary: House Democrats on the Energy and Commerce Committee are demanding answers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention regarding the agency’s refusal to accept Pennsylvania’s reporting of two measles deaths, the first in 35 years. The committee’s ranking member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) sent a letter to new agency director Erica Schwartz, calling for…
articles.body:
House Democrats on the Energy and Commerce Committee are demanding answers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention regarding the agency’s refusal to accept Pennsylvania’s reporting of two measles deaths, the first in 35 years.

The committee’s ranking member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) sent a letter to new agency director Erica Schwartz, calling for a briefing on CDC’s measles response, including why it hasn’t counted Pennsylvania’s deaths in its official weekly tally.

Pallone was joined on the letter by Reps. Diana DeGette (D-Colo), ranking member of the health subcommittee, and Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.), ranking member of the oversight and investigations subcommittee.

They are demanding a staff briefing from CDC by Sept. 28.

The decision to exclude the deaths reportedly came directly from Schwartz, who took charge of the agency this month amid a pledge to operate independently from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

As of Friday, the CDC reported 160 new measles cases in the past week, bringing this year’s total to 3,294. But according to CDC, there have been no deaths.

On its website, the agency put an asterisk next to the data and noted that the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) hasn’t recorded any deaths this year where measles was the underlying cause.

The Pennsylvania health department on Tuesday said it has now confirmed two additional measles-related deaths, bringing the state’s total to four.

“Your decision to interfere with the inclusion of the first two measles related deaths on CDC’s publicly facing database is consistent with the many other ways that the Trump Administration has degraded tools to prevent disease spread, damaged the partnership between the states and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and suppressed information about threats and harm to the public,” the Democrats wrote.

The third death “underscores the gravity of CDC’s failure to provide consistent, reliable information to the public as the country grapples with a historic return of measles,” the lawmkers wrote.

Schwartz has not publicly discussed her reasoning for excluding a state’s own reporting, a radical departure from the agency’s normal practice.

The state’s health department said it provided CDC with the relevant epidemiological data and evaluated the deaths based on CDC’s criteria.

articles.title: Cook Political Report shifts New Hampshire toward Republican Sununu
articles.summary: Cook Political Report, an election handicapper, shifted its rating for the New Hampshire Senate race to “toss-up,” a significant move in Republicans’ favor, since Democrats need to keep that seat. Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) is challenging former Sen. John Sununu (R-N.H.), who has been out of the Senate for 18 years, for the seat opening…
articles.body:
Cook Political Report, an election handicapper, shifted its rating for the New Hampshire Senate race to “toss-up,” a significant move in Republicans’ favor, since Democrats need to keep that seat.

Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) is challenging former Sen. John Sununu (R-N.H.), who has been out of the Senate for 18 years, for the seat opening up by the retirement of Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.

A late August poll by the University of New Hampshire showed Sununu and Pappas nearly tied, at 45 percent Sununu to 43 percent Pappas. While other Senate races have shifted in Democrats’ favor in recent months, New Hampshire might be an exception to a national trend. Many New Hampshire voters also favor a Republican for governor, and are generally fond of Sununu, who comes from a popular political family in the state.

“Even in a light blue state, the amount of money national Republicans have dedicated to this race is a flashing red light for Democrats,” said Jessica Taylor, editor at Cook, in a statement.

The primaries wrapped up last week, cementing Sununu and Pappas as their parties’ respective nominees. Pappas was the moderate choice in the Democratic primary, besting progressive candidate Karishma Manzur.

Sununu, who served one term in the Senate, is the brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu (R), and their father, also named John, was the state’s governor in the 1980s and chair of the state Republican party.

articles.title: Senate Democrats press Patel on elections, journalist subpoenas: 5 takeaways
articles.summary: FBI Director Kash Patel fielded questions Tuesday on everything from bestiality to whether the FBI might aid in any efforts to interfere in the upcoming midterm elections. Like his former colleague then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, he showed up to the Senate Judiciary Committee’s oversight hearing with opposition to Democratic lawmakers, though Patel largely pushed back…
articles.body:
FBI Director Kash Patel fielded questions Tuesday on everything from bestiality to whether the FBI might aid in any efforts to interfere in the upcoming midterm elections.

Like his former colleague then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, he showed up to the Senate Judiciary Committee’s oversight hearing with opposition to Democratic lawmakers, though Patel largely pushed back against Democratic attacks by boasting of arrest records, falling violent crime rates and captured most-wanted felons.

But that did not impress Democrats who see him as benefiting from already ongoing work.

“As far as I’m concerned, the good work being done by the FBI agents and analysts of the sort that you describe as happening in spite of you, not because of you,” Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) said.

Republican lawmakers generally complimented Patel on a job well done, leaving the sparring with the FBI director to the Democrats.

Growing concern over FBI involvement in elections

Numerous Democratic lawmakers pressed Patel on whether he would comply with any demands from President Trump to interfere with November’s midterms.

Patel initially told Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) he was “aware” of laws prohibiting deployment of armed federal officials to election sites as well as policy barring investigations inside polling places on Election Day.

But exchanges with other lawmakers proved more contentious and resulted in murkier answers.

“Can you commit to this committee that you will not send FBI agents to the polls on Election Day?” Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) asked.

“The FBI will follow the law. If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation of law, we will. Otherwise, we won’t,” Patel answered.

Blumenthal said he should have received an “unequivocal, clear, unambiguous commitment that the FBI will be kept out of election interference.”

Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) noted that Trump has claimed that the only way the Democrats could win the midterms is if they cheated.

“The president is completely justified in making his opinions known, as does any president before him,” Patel said, noting the FBI has election crisis coordinators in all 56 field offices.

“It’s the American people — Republicans and Democrats and Independents — who have to be the deciders of who their representatives in Congress are, not the president of the United States, not a compliant, servile FBI director who does the will of the president,” Welch said.

Subpoenas to journalists and a claim of perjury

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) accused Patel of lying about subpoenaing journalists in what turned into a lengthy exchange that prompted Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley (Iowa), chair of the committee, to raise his voice and ask the lawmaker if he was “ready to shut up.”

Booker said Patel has given inconsistent statements about the bureau’s practices, noting May testimony in which he said no journalists were being investigated while numerous subpoenas were later issued to reporters.

“Grand jury subpoenas were served on three New York Times reporters; armed FBI agents went to their homes. You subpoenaed their phone company for their call records. You subpoenaed the records of one reporter’s mother. You get upset when somebody writes a fair story about your girlfriend, but you’re out there using the FBI to go after a reporter’s mom,” Booker said, noting reporters’ spouses’ records were also sought.

Patel maintains the journalists weren’t under investigation but rather information was sought from them as part of an effort to unmask leakers providing information to journalists.

“This administration focuses on the leakers of classified information that endanger the lives of elected officials and American citizens. We are not targeting reporters at any point in time,” he said.

But the Democratic senator noted that one of the reporters whose records were subpoenaed wrote a story about Patel’s girlfriend receiving a detail composed of SWAT agents. Booker pointed to other cases where a judge had admonished the FBI for seeking subpoenas of journalists.

“None of these line up. Somewhere you’re lying. The message that every reporter in America is getting right now is that we have an FBI director that is attacking the most vaunted of our amendments, which is our first one: freedom of the press. If you write about this director, this FBI will run your name through government databases. … This man before us using a police agency to settle personal grievances about a story that embarrassed him, and this is not a one-time thing, Mr. Patel,” he said.

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) later showed a photo of Patel with a quote from him stating that the media is “the most powerful enemy the United States has ever seen.”

Patel sought to head off questions about his use of the FBI jet to travel to the 2026 Winter Olympics or to go see his country music singer girlfriend’s concerts by releasing a July 20 letter he’d written to Grassley ahead of the hearing.

“As Director, I have reimbursed all personal travel and expenses and am fully compliant with and strictly follow the Office of Management and Budget rules,” the FBI director wrote.

Compared with past appearances before Congress, Patel received fewer questions about his travels.

Hirono noted that a VIP snorkel trip at the site of the USS Arizona in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, is “a sacred site. Sacred. That is why these tours are rare.”

“As part of a broader pattern of you using your office to benefit yourself, showing your lack of judgment and character, you have wasted untold taxpayer dollars driving around in foreign luxury cars, partying in Italy, and flying a private jet to play golf and watch hockey. There has been bipartisan criticism. I’m glad to know that some of my Republican colleagues actually criticized some of this activity,” she said.

Patel grew defensive when asked about his trip to Italy for the Winter Olympics by Welch, who noted photos of the FBI director partying with the U.S. men’s national hockey team in their locker room.

“What you’ll never understand is the players who are my friends invited me into the locker room. What you’ll never understand is that during that trip — where 300,000 Americans went to Italy to participate in the games and watched them — not a single security incident occurred,” Patel said before going on to reference the extradition of a man held in Italy.

“And the most important thing to come out of that trip, besides the American men defeating the Canadians and celebrating the love of this country and inviting me in to do so is the fact that we obtained the seizure and capture of China’s most prolific hacker and returned him to the United States.”

Patel refused to answer several questions posed by Democratic lawmakers, routinely citing ongoing investigations.

He would not answer questions about a Florida-based federal investigation into a number of perceived Trump enemies, including into former CIA Director John Brennan, as well as investigations that included subpoenas of journalists to various shootings carried out by immigration officers.

Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), who questioned the director about immigration-related shootings, asked, “Why does it take so long?” when Patel said he was unable to answer.

“I know some of these shootings and incidents have been more recent, but some go back months and months and months, some to last year,” Padilla said.

Hirono seemed to reference Patel’s posts announcing the arrests of shooters following the assassination of Charlie Kirk and a shooting at Brown University.

“You know you testified today that to questions you don’t feel like answering — ‘It’s ongoing. It’s an investigation. Can’t talk about it.’ And yet you have actually posted things that should be ongoing and where you should keep your mouth shut,” she said.

In one notable exchange , Patel was asked about a shift in FBI hiring practices that lifted longtime bans on selecting new trainees if they have engaged in prostitution or bestiality.

“When you saw bestiality — I say this with respect to the person who recommended it — why didn’t you just say, ‘What planet did you parachute in from? Why do I want to lead with my chin and get into bestiality?’” Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) asked.

Patel acknowledged he had some reservations but said prospective hires could have been trafficked into “degrading acts of all kinds.”

“That was my initial response, senator. But they then explained to me and showed me cases in which people were forced into it and had applied to the FBI, and so I thought they should be considered. It’s not an automatic disqualification. That’s all,” the director said.

Those activities have long been a bar to working at the FBI, as engaging in prostitution is a crime and the FBI works on sex trafficking cases. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), the Senate Judiciary Committee’s ranking member, earlier this week said lifting the ban on animal cruelty is not a “minor technical adjustment.”

“But you’re not telling us today that if a human being had sex with an animal, that they can still be an FBI agent,” Kennedy asked toward the end of his line of questioning.

articles.title: US speaker rejects AI pause, warns of losing edge to China
articles.summary: Trump has dismissed AI fears as ‘hoax’, insisting US safeguards suffice and warning slowdown benefits China.
articles.body:
US House Speaker Mike Johnson has rejected calls to pause artificial intelligence development, arguing that doing so could give China an advantage over the United States.

“We cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI,” Johnson told reporters on Tuesday. “Because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for every American family.”

Johnson also argued that AI companies should largely be left to police themselves.

“They can self-regulate. They don’t need the government to tell them to slow it down. If they want to slow it down, they should,” he said.

His comments come as calls to rein in AI are growing across the political spectrum amid concerns about what the technology could mean for jobs, energy costs and public safety.

Unlikely allies US Senator Bernie Sanders, a self-described democratic socialist, and Steve Bannon, a former adviser to President Donald Trump and prominent voice on the US right, both called for restrictions on AI on Tuesday, as they appeared at the same event in Washington.

Sanders warned of what he called the “growing threat” of AI and said the industry should face binding safety rules.

“AI has the potential to eliminate tens of millions of jobs, wiping out entire professions and making it harder for our young people to enter the workforce,” he said.

He criticised tech executives, including Elon Musk, for concentrating control over the technology.

“As many scientists believe could happen, this technology will escape human control with potentially catastrophic consequences,” Sanders said.

He cited recent research in which scientists used AI to design new viruses, a breakthrough that has raised concerns about potential biosecurity risks, adding that “in the wrong hands, this could lead to new bioweapons and a potential global pandemic that could lead to the deaths of tens of millions of people”.

Sanders also called on Trump to use his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping to negotiate a treaty to pause AI development.

Bannon called AI “the defining issue of our time” and said the US needed to slow its development to understand the risks, praising Sanders’ description of the risks and arguing the issue needed to transcend partisan politics.

“I don’t think you could find any two harder partisans than Bernie Sanders on the left and Steve Bannon on the right,” he said.

On Monday, Trump downplayed concerns raised by industry leaders about the potential misuse of AI, saying the US already has safeguards in place.

In a series of posts, he dismissed fears that AI could pose an existential threat as a “ hoax ” and argued that existing government powers were enough to keep companies in check.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT,” Trump wrote, adding: “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”

He also accused critics of AI and data centres of engaging in a “sick conspiracy”, arguing that efforts to slow the industry would ultimately benefit China.

Speaker Johnson, who echoed Trump’s concerns about falling behind China on Tuesday, did leave some room for guardrails, saying they would have to be put in place in a balanced and thoughtful way.

“I think you need independent auditors. I think you need transparency from the people who are developing this,” he said.

Johnson also said he spoke to Trump on Monday night and that executives from major AI companies would be summoned to the White House for a meeting within the next week.

articles.title: Fetterman again says he’s ‘not going to be a Republican’ following RNC convention video appearance
articles.summary: Sen. John Fetterman (D-Penn.) again emphasized that he would not be switching parties Tuesday following his video appearance at the Republican National Committee (RNC) midterm convention. When asked by a reporter at Capitol Hill if there was a chance he would become a Republican, Fetterman appeared to become frustrated. “I’m not going to be a…
articles.body:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Penn.) again emphasized that he would not be switching parties Tuesday following his video appearance at the Republican National Committee (RNC) midterm convention.

When asked by a reporter at Capitol Hill if there was a chance he would become a Republican, Fetterman appeared to become frustrated.

“I’m not going to be a Republican. Why can’t you guys just wait till the midterms? And if I turn a Republican, then I’ll be a liar,” he said. “My name is not on the ballot. Chill.”

“I’ve always been a Democrat. It’s like, no matter how many times I say that, I’m still getting asked just getting into the elevator,” the lawmaker added.

Democratic colleagues grew frustrated with Fetterman following a video he made introducing his fellow Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick (R) at the GOP midterm convention — describing him as a “ great friend .”

The pair have built a close relationship as earlier in the summer they launched a joint political action committee, Common Ground PA , seeking to target donors who support both lawmakers.

Fetterman said in a statement after the video’s release that he would continue to caucus with Democrats, writing last week, “I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party—and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on.”

Despite the criticism from his own party, Fetterman votes with the Democratic caucus 90 percent of the time — something that he mentions when asked about whether he would leave the party — but he has also split from Democrats on high-profile votes.

This includes the Iran war as Fetterman voted against every Senate war powers resolution introduced in the upper chamber.

Fetterman has said previously at the Hill Nation Summit that he would leave the Democratic Party if it turned its back on Israel entirely.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz have already indicated they would welcome Fetterman to the GOP.

articles.title: Ohio city council decides to rename Lake Erie to ‘Gulf of Cleveland’
articles.summary: The Cleveland, Ohio, City Council on Monday voted to rename a portion of Lake Erie as the “Gulf of Cleveland,” taking a jab at President Trump’s executive order declaring that Lake Ontario be called the “Gulf of America.” The emergency resolution led by Councilmember Kris Harsh passed in a 13-1 vote and was intended to…
articles.body:
The Cleveland, Ohio, City Council on Monday voted to rename a portion of Lake Erie as the “Gulf of Cleveland,” taking a jab at President Trump’s executive order declaring that Lake Ontario be called the “Gulf of America.”

The emergency resolution led by Councilmember Kris Harsh passed in a 13-1 vote and was intended to take effect immediately. The resolution is not legally binding.

Harsh’s speech to attendees ahead of the vote referred to Trump’s order to rename Lake Ontario, as well as ordering the Gulf of Mexico be called “ the Gulf of America ” last year, and his recent suggestion of calling New Mexico “ New America ” after a viral social media post falsely claimed he signed such an executive order.

The resolution applies to the 2-mile stretch of water from the city shoreline, from its eastern to its western borders. It additionally requires the city clerk to notify Apple and other national mapping companies about this new name.

“President Trump’s orders to assign new names without reference to history, tradition, and other acts of Congress have opened the door for United States officials to rename other geography,” Harsh said. “Thanks to him, this is a man who clearly isn’t afraid to say what no one is thinking.”

Harsh added that Trump’s moves made him “emboldened” to rename Cleveland’s neighboring Great Lake. He held up a map during his speech that showed “Gulf of Cleveland” written over the portion of the lake closest to the city.

Harsh also speculated on any pushback to the renaming before replying to that hypothetical pushback with “Who cares?”

“Listen to me very carefully and jot this down: Words don’t matter,” he added, later mocking Trump’s style of ending Truth Social posts by saying at the end of his own speech: “Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

Trump’s orders to rename Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico were quickly integrated into Google’s and Apple’s online maps and visible to users in the U.S. International users saw both names, while Canadian and Mexican users, respectively, saw the commonly used names of both bodies of water on the platforms.

It also prompted MapQuest downloads to soar, as the company left the names of both bodies of water unchanged.

Google’s change applied to the Gulf of Mexico led the U.S.’s southern neighbor to sue the tech giant in May 2025. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum had warned months earlier that changing the Gulf’s name violated her country’s sovereignty .

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford pushed back on Trump’s order earlier this month, as the move came on the heels of the trade war between the two countries. Ford said the move resembled “something out of ‘Saturday Night Live.'”

The Seneca Nation also called on Trump to reverse the order , stating that it violated the 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua, which established the nation’s territorial borders.

articles.title: Democrats favored over Republicans on health care, immigration, economy: Survey

articles.body:
Democrats are ahead of Republicans on some of the issues most important to voters —immigration, health care and the economy—according to a new poll.

In the New York Times/Siena University poll , 51 percent of likely voter respondents said they trusted Democrats to excel in their work on the economy over Republicans, while 45 percent said the same of Republicans in comparison to Democrats and 4 percent were unsure or did not answer the question.

When it came to the topic of immigration, 52 percent of respondents backed Democrats’ performance over Republicans, while 45 percent backed Republicans over Democrats and 3 percent were unsure or did not answer the question.

And when it came to health care, 60 percent of respondents backed Democrats’ performance over Republicans, while 36 percent backed Republicans over Democrats and 5 percent were unsure or did not answer the question.

The Times/Siena poll spells trouble for Republicans as the midterms elections are only a few weeks out. The party is already dealing with issues like President Trump’s slumping approval rating, the unpopular war in Iran that is nearing its seventh month and Democrats recently excelling on the generic congressional ballot.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 39.5 percent as of late Tuesday afternoon, while his disapproval rating was at 58.2 percent.

However, a top political adviser to Trump recently said he was “cautiously optimistic” that Republicans can hold onto Congress.

“I won’t predict, you know, how many seats are going to be in either chamber come November,” James Blair told NBC News’s podcast, “Here’s the Scoop: Election Edition.” “But, I do think there is a path for us to retain both majorities and defy history.”

The Times/Siena poll took place between Sept. 8 and 13, featuring 1,503 likely voters and a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.

articles.title: Democrats want to investigate Russian influence in Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding
articles.summary: A Democratic senator is pressing the Trump administration to look into reports that a Russian oligarch paid for wedding celebrations for Donald Trump Jr., the son of President Donald Trump. Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who has traveled frequently to Ukraine amid its war with Russia, brought up the issue during a hearing Tuesday while questioning…
articles.body:
A Democratic senator is pressing the Trump administration to look into reports that a Russian oligarch paid for wedding celebrations for Donald Trump Jr., the son of President Donald Trump.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who has traveled frequently to Ukraine amid its war with Russia, brought up the issue during a hearing Tuesday while questioning FBI Director Kash Patel.

Patel denied that the reports were necessarily accurate and said he did not review them before the hearing Tuesday morning.

“You’re referring to something that happened yesterday in public reporting, and public reporting generally isn’t accurate,” said Patel, saying the FBI would look at “whatever information comes our way.”

Blumenthal asked Patel to report back to the Senate Judiciary Committee with steps the FBI was taking to investigate improper influence by Kremlev.

“I was surprised beyond words,” Blumenthal later told The Hill about the reporting. “I was absolutely astonished and appalled that a Russian oligarch with ties to Vladimir Putin is bankrolling the president’s son’s wedding. It’s beyond belief.”

ProPublica reported Monday that a wealthy Russian businessman named Umar Kremlev, who has close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, paid for and attended lavish wedding celebrations for Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Anderson, on a private island in the Bahamas in May.

Anderson in a post on Instagram said the festivities were not the wedding itself, but confirmed that Kremlev is a “dear friend” who hosted two nights of “celebrations” as a gift.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, at a White House press briefing on Tuesday, dismissed the idea that an investigation was needed, saying he didn’t know “this person” Kremlev and neither did Trump.

“Am I investigating what? And when you say, this person is a friend of Putin, I don’t even know whether that’s true or not,” Blanche said in response to a reporter’s question. “I think all the relevant people involved, the president and his kids have already addressed it, I don’t have any information, I don’t know this person either.”

Democrats in the House are also clamoring for answers on whether there was compromised intelligence or other unethical exchanges as a result of the friendship between the couple and Kremlev.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) told reporters Monday that the Trump family “are in the pocket of everyone but the American people.”

“I said it two years ago, and I’m saying it again. This administration … they are selling out every single person in this country for a buck, and it’s disgusting. And for what? To have a couple of extra frills at your wedding?”

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, posted on social media in response to the ProPublica story that he wanted more information on any quid pro quo Kremlev might have received from the Trump family.

“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” Garcia wrote . “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”

Republicans in Congress were generally not focused on the situation on Monday and Tuesday. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) told The Hill that his constituents are not talking about the Trump wedding.

“I heard about the thing, and same time we’re talking affordability back home, and we’re talking cattle prices back home,” Rounds said. “His wedding was a pretty low priority.”
