articles.title: 64 House Democrats help Republicans kill Trump impeachment effort
articles.summary: Al Green forced a Trump impeachment vote that fractured House Democrats, with Hakeem Jeffries and top leaders voting "present" to avoid taking a stand.
articles.body: Dozens of House Democrats voted to help Republicans quash an effort to impeach President Donald Trump on Tuesday. Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, forced a vote on impeaching Trump over federal immigration officials' killing of two U.S. citizens earlier this year. The move fractured House Democrats, whose leaders have largely avoided placing an emphasis on trying to oust the president as they work to take back Congress in the November midterms. The House voted to table the measure in a 232 to 147 vote, a maneuver to get rid of it while avoiding voting on the impeachment resolution itself. Eighteen House Democrats voted with Republicans to table the resolution, while 46 voted "present." Nearly 150 voted to move forward with a vote on impeaching Trump. OUTGOING HOUSE DEMOCRAT AL GREEN FILES ANOTHER IMPEACHMENT RESOLUTION TARGETING PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP Democrats walked a political tightrope with the bill, forced to choose between appeasing their anti-Trump base and appealing to moderate and independent voters by showing them they were focused on tackling Americans' everyday issues like high cost of living rather than political revenge. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and his top deputies voted "present," avoiding taking a stand on the matter while allowing Republicans to more easily scuttle the resolution. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: DEM REBELS EXPOSE CRACKS IN JEFFRIES’ HOUSE LEADERSHIP Jeffries said in a statement that impeachment "traditionally requires a comprehensive investigative process, the collection and review of thousands of documents, an exacting scrutiny of the facts, the examination of dozens of key witnesses, congressional hearings, sustained public organizing and the marshaling of the forces of democracy to build a broad national consensus." "None of that serious work has been done, with the Republican majority focused solely on rubber-stamping Donald Trump’s extreme agenda," senior House Democratic leaders said. "Accordingly, we will again vote 'present' on the motion to table the impeachment resolution as we continue our fight to make life more affordable for everyday Americans, while committing to holding the crooks accountable using every tool available to us beginning on day one." But Green railed against Jeffries and other Democrats who did not vote to impeach Trump during his own comments to reporters on Monday. "They will acknowledge that what the president is doing is impeachable, but they would have us wait. Well, the Constitution doesn't have a wait clause in it," Green said. "I believe that there are some Republicans and Democrats who are considering voting to protect the president. If they're not considering protecting him, that will be the effect of what they will do when they vote to either table or they vote to send this to a committee for further investigation." CONSERVATIVES ERUPT AFTER AL GREEN MELTS DOWN DURING VIRAL CLASH: 'UNHINGED LUNATIC' Green previously forced a vote to impeach Trump in June 2025, when 128 Democrats joined Republicans in voting to table the Texas progressive's resolution. articles.title: House sinks Al Green bid to impeach Trump
articles.summary: House lawmakers voted Tuesday to sink a Democratic effort to impeach President Trump over the administration’s aggressive deportation agenda. Sponsored by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas), the resolution accused Trump of abusing his powers by launching an immigration crackdown that led to the killing of several civilians earlier in the year. The vote was 232-147 to…
articles.body:
House lawmakers voted Tuesday to sink a Democratic effort to impeach President Trump over the administration’s aggressive deportation agenda.

Sponsored by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas), the resolution accused Trump of abusing his powers by launching an immigration crackdown that led to the killing of several civilians earlier in the year.

The vote was 232-147 to shelve the measure, with eighteen Democrats joining almost every Republican in voting to table the resolution, including Reps. Henry Cuellar (Texas), Jared Golden (Maine), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.), Jared Moskowitz (Fla.), Kathy Castor (Fla.) and Emanuel Cleaver (Mo.).

Forty-seven lawmakers voted “present,” including the top Democratic leaders: Reps. Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), Katherine Clark (Mass.) and Pete Aguilar (Calif.).

Democratic leaders said their noncommittal votes reflected the fact that the impeachment articles were brought to the floor without any formal investigations, hearings or broader examination of the charges they contained.

“None of that serious work has been done, with the Republican majority focused solely on rubber stamping Donald Trump’s extreme agenda,” the Democratic leaders said Monday night in a joint statement.

But there are other reasons for their cautious approach.

Democrats are bullish about their chances of flipping control of the House in November’s midterms, and they want to keep a disciplined focus on the volatile economy and high cost of living under Trump’s second term, which they see as the best message for achieving that goal.

Impeachment, while supported by many liberals, also risks distracting from the broader economic message, which has a better chance of resonating with moderate and independent voters who might want a check on Trump, but don’t support ousting him altogether.

Some Democrats are also worried that impeaching Trump would only animate the president’s supporters to get to the polls, making it tougher for Democrats to flip the House in the midterms.

Heading into Tuesday’s vote, Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), the chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, further distanced party leaders from the resolution.

“This is something oftentimes I think the right-wing media wants us to talk about,” Aguilar said. “But it’s not anything that’s top of the agenda for House Democrats.”

Green, for his part, has been undeterred. A 22-year House veteran and staunch liberal representing Houston, he says Trump’s actions have left him no choice but to pursue impeachment. A failure to do so, he says, would send the message to future presidents that Trump’s actions did not rise to the level of impeachment.

“The issue isn’t whether the President is guilty of impeachable offenses, because he is,” Green wrote last week to his House colleagues urging their support. “The super salient issue is: What will the U.S. House of Representatives (which has the sole power to impeach) do about it?”

Green’s impeachment articles focused on the administration’s deportation surge earlier in the year, when members of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) conducted aggressive raids around the country in search of undocumented immigrants.

In the course of those operations, federal enforcement officers killed a handful of civilians, including Renée Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis; Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston; and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine.

The administration has defended the killings, saying federal officers feared for their lives in each instance and were merely acting in self defense — an argument disputed by the victims’ relatives, camera footage or both.

Green’s impeachment articles named those victims, accusing the president of “operating vicious, quota-driven, unaccountable paramilitary forces killing people.”

“President Trump, using the powers of his high office, individually and in coordination with officers in his administration, has transformed ICE and CBP into dangerous, unaccountable paramilitary police forces that operate without oversight and pose a direct threat to the constitutional order of the United States and the people of the United States,” the articles read.

“By such abuses of power, President Trump is brazenly and wantonly devolving the United States democratic republic into an authoritarian regime.”

Green is no stranger to clashes with Trump. Under the president’s first term, Green was among the first Democrats to pursue impeachment, even when party leaders remained cold to the idea. (They would eventually change their tune, voting twice to impeach Trump during his first term).

More recently, Green made waves in the Capitol for heckling Trump during his appearances before joint sessions of Congress in both 2025 and 2026. For the earlier incident, House lawmakers voted to censure Green .

The outbursts have frustrated some Democrats in the Capitol, who want the party to stay focused on kitchen table economics. Those critics need not worry about another round of Green impeachment resolutions next year. In May, the longtime Democrat lost his primary , a victim of the Republicans’ national redistricting campaign.

Voters in the First State head to the polls on Tuesday for the Democratic and Republican primaries for their lone U.S. House seat.

First-term Rep. Sarah McBride (D-Del.) begins her reelection effort running unopposed in the Democratic primary after taking over the seat from now-Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) in 2025. McBride is the first transgender person to serve in Congress.

Three Republicans are running in the primary to challenge McBride, including her former opponent in the 2024 Democratic primary and Republican nominee she defeated in 2024.

Earl Cooper, who received 16 percent of the vote in that primary to McBride’s 80 percent, is seeking a rematch but running as a Republican. He’ll first have to get past medical doctor Joseph Arminio and retired business owner John J. Whalen, who was the 2024 Republican nominee for the seat against McBride.

articles.title: Pennsylvania reports teen as fourth measles death amid feud with RFK Jr.
articles.summary: Pennsylvania officials on Tuesday reported two additional measles-related deaths, bringing the total for the year to four. This is a record-setting year for measles in the U.S. The number of cases is at a 35-year high and there are more deaths than any year since 1992. The newest death according to state health officials was…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania officials on Tuesday reported two additional measles-related deaths, bringing the total for the year to four.

This is a record-setting year for measles in the U.S. The number of cases is at a 35-year high and there are more deaths than any year since 1992.

The newest death according to state health officials was an unvaccinated person who lived in Mifflin County, located in Central Pennsylvania. County coroner Andrea L. Alcalde in a news release said an 18-year-old died from acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a “rare and severe neurological complication of measles.”

The coroner did not release any other details, including when the person died.

The state health department also confirmed a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County died from measles complications. County officials first reported the death over the weekend.

In late August, state officials announced the state’s first measles-associated deaths in 35 years in Lancaster County. The county coroner later disclosed that it was two infants who died.

One of the deaths he attributed directly to measles, while the other died shortly after birth from a ruptured spleen. The coroner said measles contributed to that death, but was not a direct cause.

The state said that it has now confirmed 693 cases of measles in 38 counties in this year’s outbreak. Nationally, more than 3,200 measles cases have been reported.

“My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly-contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades,” Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen said in a statement.

“We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the MMR vaccine – which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades,” Bogen said.

The best protection against measles remains getting fully vaccinated, according to the Pennsylvania Health Department as well as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The MMR vaccine, administered over two doses, boosts a person’s immune system and provides 97 percent lifetime protection.

Measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, but cases are surging due to low vaccination rates, and the U.S. is at risk of losing that elimination status.

“These are tragedies, and four families are grieving,” Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) wrote Tuesday on X.

The announcement of the additional deaths comes amid an ongoing bitter political feud between Shapiro, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The feud continued Tuesday, when Shapiro lashed out at Kennedy.

“This serious situation continues to be made worse by RFK Jr. playing games with public health and safety. It’s long past time for @SecKennedy to stop stoking vaccine skepticism and misinformation and compromising the serious mission of the nation’s public health agencies,” Shapiro wrote.

Kennedy in turn blamed Shapiro for politicizing the outbreak.

“He continues to point the finger at me and the federal government and to malign the Amish while refusing the federal assistance that might help end the outbreak,” Kennedy wrote on X.

“I have offered the Governor CDC Epi-Aid, which would put CDC epidemiologists on the ground to help the state respond. Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin requested Epi-Aids and worked alongside CDC teams to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control,” Kennedy wrote.

But states don’t always request epi-aids. For instance, Utah had a recent measles outbreak but Kennedy did not mention whether officials there had asked for assistance.

Meanwhile, the CDC has been excluding the two Lancaster County deaths from its weekly updates of a national measles death tally, a radical departure from the typical agency practice of accepting a state’s own reporting.

The decision to exclude the deaths reportedly came from the CDC’s new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, at the behest of Kennedy.

Shapiro on Tuesday called out Kennedy’s role in deciding against counting the deaths.

“It is also deeply concerning to learn that the Secretary personally intervened in an otherwise administrative process to direct the CDC to not report these Pennsylvania deaths, presumably because it doesn’t fit his phony narrative,” Shapiro wrote.

Kennedy denied CDC was trying to suppress the information, and said the agency was merely “applying a consistent national standard rather than allowing politicians to decide which deaths appear in federal mortality statistics.”
